moduleMetadata.title: Phishing & Social Engineering
moduleMetadata.description: Learn to recognize the signs of phishing and social engineering attacks that target people rather than technical systems.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Attackers do not always need to break through sophisticated technical defenses. Sometimes, they try to manipulate people into making the security mistake for them.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should be able to recognize common phishing and social-engineering indicators.

learningObjectives: Define phishing and its various forms (email, smishing, vishing).
Identify common psychological tactics like urgency, fear, and authority.
Recognize red flags in emails, messages, and calls.
Apply verification techniques to suspicious communications.
Understand the risks of fake login pages and malicious attachments.

sections.title: What is Phishing?
sections.content: Phishing is a type of social engineering where an attacker sends a fraudulent message designed to trick a person into revealing sensitive information or deploying malicious software.

subsections.title: Email Phishing
subsections.content: The most common form. Attackers send emails that look like they come from a trusted source (bank, manager, tech support).

subsections.title: Smishing (SMS Phishing)
subsections.content: Phishing attempts sent via text message.

subsections.title: Vishing (Voice Phishing)
subsections.content: Phishing attempts made over the phone.

sections.title: The Psychology of an Attack
sections.content: Attackers use human emotions to make you act quickly without thinking.
bulletPoints: Authority: 'I am the CEO, and I need this done immediately.'
Curiosity: 'You won't believe what's in this attachment!'

sections.title: Spotting Red Flags
sections.content: Look for these indicators of a phishing attempt:
list: Mismatched sender address (e.g., support@paypa1.com instead of paypal.com).
Suspicious links (hover over a link to see the real destination).

sections.title: Fake Login Pages
sections.content: Attackers create websites that look exactly like a real login page (e.g., Office 365 or a bank). When you enter your credentials, they are stolen.
sections.tip: Always check the URL in the browser's address bar before typing your password.

interactiveExercises.title: Spot the Phish
interactiveExercises.question: You receive an email from 'Service@Amazon.net' stating your recent order for a $900 TV cannot be shipped. It asks you to click a link to 'verify your billing info'. What is the biggest red flag?
options: The font used in the email.
The fact that it's about an order.
interactiveExercises.explanation: Attackers use look-alike domains to appear legitimate.

interactiveExercises.title: Phishing and Message Checker
interactiveExercises.instruction: Paste the content of a suspicious message into the tool to analyze its risk level.

scenarios.title: 15-Minute Suspension
scenarios.content: An email claims your student account will be suspended in 15 minutes unless you verify your password and MFA code immediately via a link.
scenarios.action: Delete the email or report it. Never click links in high-urgency emails. Go to the official portal directly.
scenarios.lesson: Extreme time pressure is a classic phishing tactic.

scenarios.title: The Bank SMS
scenarios.content: A text message says: 'Your bank account is closed. Click here to reactivate: bit.ly/fake-bank'.
scenarios.action: Do not click. Banks will not send account closure notices with shortened links via SMS.
scenarios.lesson: Smishing often uses shortened links to hide the real destination.

scenarios.title: The OTP Voice Call
scenarios.content: A caller says they are from 'Fraud Detection' and they need the One-Time Password (OTP) sent to your phone to 'secure' your account.
scenarios.action: Hang up. Legitimate companies will never call and ask for an OTP that they sent to you.
scenarios.lesson: Vishing attempts to steal MFA codes through social pressure.

scenarios.title: The CEO's Urgent Favor
scenarios.content: The Director sends a DM: 'I'm in a meeting. Can you bypass the normal procedure and send me the confidential sales report for last year immediately?'
scenarios.action: Verify through a different channel (e.g., call them or wait for the meeting to end).
scenarios.lesson: Authority impersonation tries to make you ignore security procedures.

quiz.question: What is 'Smishing'?
quiz.explanation: Smishing uses text messages to deliver fraudulent content.

quiz.question: When you hover your mouse over a link in an email, what should you look for?
options: The actual destination URL shown at the bottom of the window.
How many words are in the link.
If the link has a 'click here' button.
quiz.correctAnswer: The actual destination URL shown at the bottom of the window.
quiz.explanation: Hovering reveals where the link will actually take you, which may differ from what is written.

quiz.question: Which of these is a common 'Psychological Trigger' used by attackers?
options: Offering to help you with chores
quiz.explanation: Urgency stops people from thinking critically about the request.

quiz.question: Is a 'Dear Valued Customer' greeting a sign of a legitimate personalized email?
options: No, it is a generic greeting often used in bulk phishing.
quiz.correctAnswer: No, it is a generic greeting often used in bulk phishing.
quiz.explanation: Legitimate services you have an account with will usually address you by name.

quiz.question: What is the best way to verify a suspicious email from your bank?
options: Reply to the email and ask if it's real.
Click the link in the email and see if it looks professional.
Call the bank's official number from their website or your card.
Ask a friend what they think.
quiz.correctAnswer: Call the bank's official number from their website or your card.
quiz.explanation: Verify through an 'out-of-band' or trusted secondary channel.

quiz.question: Social engineering is an attack on:
quiz.explanation: It relies on manipulating people into making security mistakes.

quiz.question: What is the risk of opening an unexpected attachment?
options: It might be a large file and slow down your computer.
It might contain malware that infects your system.
It might be a boring document.
It might be a gift from a stranger.
quiz.correctAnswer: It might contain malware that infects your system.
quiz.explanation: Attachments are a primary delivery method for viruses and ransomware.

keyTakeaways: Phishing can happen via email, text, or phone call.
Be skeptical of any message that creates intense urgency or fear.
Always verify the sender's real address and link destinations.
Never share passwords or MFA codes over the phone or in a message.
reflectApply: Look at your spam folder. Can you identify three red flags in the most recent phishing attempt there?
If you received an 'urgent' call from your manager today, how would you verify it was really them before sharing data?
